item.title: Gray 'will continue until told otherwise' - but has Hibs boss lost the fans?
item.description: Head coach David Gray says he will continue to try and find solutions to Hibernian's poor form "until someone was to say something different" after his side suffered a sixth consecutive home defeat in the Scottish Premiership.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Head coach David Gray says he will continue to try and find solutions to Hibernian's poor form "until someone was to say something different" after his side suffered a sixth consecutive home defeat in the Scottish Premiership.

Kilmarnock secured their first league win of the season thanks to George Stanger's first-half goal at Easter Road and held on despite a late red card.

The boos that echoed round the stadium were in stark contrast to Saturday, when Hibs eased aside League 1 pacesetters Ross County 3-0 to set up a League Cup semi-final against city rivals Hearts.

But club legend Gray realises that the latest league defeat, their fourth in six games overall, will see pressure mount, with his team now sitting ninth.

"It's clear to see, it's not good enough in terms of the result," the former Hibs right-back and Scottish Cup-winning captain told BBC Scotland.

"Nobody wants to hear me stand here and talk about the tactical side of the game at this moment in time. We have lost a game again at home.

"The only way it turns is by putting yourself out there, sticking together and believing in yourself and trusting your ability.

"One thing I will continue to do is work as hard as I can to turn this around. I've been through adversity before at this football club and I will continue until someone tells me otherwise. I believe in my group and believe in what we're doing.

"Until someone was to say something different, I will continue to do everything to turn this around."

Is Aberdeen visit a 'must-win'?

For former Hibs midfielder Scott Allan, Saturday's visit by Aberdeen is now "a must-win" for former team-mate Gray.

"This won't go down well with the Hibs faithful," he said on BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound. "It's the manner they lost, the level of performance, the amount of duels they lost, how easily it was for Kilmarnock to play through them.

"It was genuinely incredible at times, while going the other way they hardly created anything of note. That will not be accepted by the Hibs fans and certainly not David Gray."

When asked what is going wrong at Easter Road, former Scotland forward James McFadden said if he knew that, he would "phone David Gray and tell him".

"They are not starting games well, they are having to make changes, not making an impact," McFadden said on Sportscene.

"They couldn't find the breakthrough against a Kilmarnock side who have been leaking goals, but that's credit to Kilmarnock for the way they defended.

"Nobody can complain about Kilmarnock winning that game tonight. It is tough times ahead for Hibs."

Have the fans turned against club legend?

Kieron: Kilmarnock could have won by three or four and it wouldn't of flattered them. Hibs were so poor tonight. David Gray's position is hanging by a thread.

Stuart: The players on that pitch have to take as much responsibility as Gray for this result, nowhere near good enough. Amateur performance.

Andy: How can Gray continue to keep his job? The players are not playing for him. The club is a mess. Banning the only fans that bring an atmosphere. Benching three of our best players. So confusing.

Chris: Question the tactics. Thought for long time long ball is desperate and lacks ambition. Pressure indeed on David Gray.

Lee: If we end the game two points off bottom spot then it's surely time up for the Hibs manager. It's not a run and recovery from a bad position needed, it's deliver and results from the get go the support demands for a club of our size.

Stuart: The players on that pitch have to take as much responsibility as David Gray for this result, nowhere near good enough. Amateur performance.

Paul: Long balls to no-one as usual from Hibs and as usual our keeper is a weak link. Gray has to go even if we win as this is awful football. Bring in Neil Lennon or Steve Clarke asap before our season drifts to nothing as usual.

Andy: How can Gray continue to keep his job? The players are not playing for him. The club is a mess. Banning the only fans that bring an atmosphere. Benching three of our best players. So confusing.

Brian: Worst backline in Scotland, midfielders trot about like headless chickens, feel sorry for strikers. Gray clueless. No plan. No tactics. Blah, blah, blah after game as usual but won't resign. Board have to act.

SMcDhfc: David Gray has lost the team, it was obvious tonight. As an attacking force, we were shocking, lots of huffing and puffing but not one real effort on target. The players should be embarrassed after that display, but they will get the result they are after, Gray sacked.

Craig: I like Gray but believe it's time he goes. He has one formation. It's just not good enough. But, if he goes, Malky MacKay [director of football] should go too. His signings have been terrible.

item.title: Let them ref the games and be humans - Andrews
item.description: After Brentford overcame Reading to reach the Carabao Cup fourth round, head coach Keith Andrews believes the video assistant referee (VAR) is preventing referees from making decisions in matches.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Brentford head coach Keith Andrews believes the video assistant referee (VAR) is preventing referees from making decisions in matches.

As his Bees progressed to the Carabao Cup fourth round with a battling 2-1 win at League One side Reading, Andrews said he was not happy with the officiating.

Reading defender Paudie O'Connor had a goal for a first-half overhead kick ruled out by referee Tom Nield for a high boot, prompting Royals boss Leam Richardson to say it was "possibly in the top three [wrong] decisions that I've seen in my career - and I've seen thousands of games and played in hundreds".

With no VAR used at this stage of the EFL Cup, Andrews added: "It's been a tough week for officials as everybody is probably aware.

"I think we just need to let them ref the game and be human beings and make decisions.

"We have gone through a period in the game where I feel like they weren't actually making decisions in both boxes because of the technology we have in the game and I feel like that is a real shame."

His comments followed the admission of Pro Ref to an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's winning goal for Manchester City in their Premier League encounter at Manchester United on Sunday.

There was intense debate over whether the goal should have been disallowed for City midfielder Enzo Fernandez - who was in an offside position - interfering with play as he dived, attempting to head the ball in a central position before Haaland's finish.

Andrews, whose Brentford side are seventh in the Premier League, said referees were no longer allowed to "make mistakes".

"I always felt as a player, when there was a relationship with an official that was built on respect and being able to speak to each other in a certain way," he added.

"We've gone away from allowing them to officiate and allowing them to make mistakes and I think it is a real shame.

"Now they are having to go back to that and it's not the habits they have had in recent years."

On Sunday's refereeing error in the Manchester derby, Andrews said it was "pretty alarming" Haaland's goal was allowed to stand.

"The first thing was whether [Erling] Haaland was offside and then obviously [Enzo] Fernandez was. It's a shame," he admitted.

item.title: Messi in Argentina squad for farewell friendly
item.description: Argentina name Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Argentina have named Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.

Messi announced his retirement from Argentina duty in August in the wake of his country's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final and after saying he was considering his future in football following the death of his father, Jorge.

The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina when they won the 2022 World Cup, said the decision to stop playing for La Albiceleste hurt him "deeply" but that he had "given it my all" and had "nothing left to give".

Messi, an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner who currently plays for Inter Miami, is Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player, having scored 125 goals in 207 appearances.

"We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on 6 October here in Argentina," said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.

River Plate's Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which has an 85,000 capacity, will host the game against Benin.

Argentina's 2022 World Cup winners have also been invited to the match, which Tapia said would be an "unforgettable" occasion.

Argentina were ordered to play their next two home matches with 50% capacity, although one match of that sanction was suspended, for breaches of the Fifa disciplinary code during the World Cup.

The punishment related to using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, team misconduct, and discriminatory chants and gestures by its supporters.

After defeating England 2-1 in the World Cup semi-final, several Argentina players held up a banner claiming Argentine sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory.

As they play friendlies against Bolivia on 30 September in Cordoba and Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires on 3 October, it should mean the punishment will have been served before the Benin game.

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes and team-mate Nahuel Molina are not expected to be available as they were given respective 10-game and seven-match suspensions for their part in on-field clashes following their country's defeat by Spain in the World Cup final.

item.title: 'Superstar' Dowman shows his class - but Arsenal know caution is needed
item.description: Max Dowman shines with two goals against Ipswich Town - but boss Mikel Arteta warns Arsenal cannot rush his development.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Arsenal teenager Max Dowman shone with two goals in the 4-2 Carabao Cup win over Ipswich Town - but boss Mikel Arteta warned they cannot rush his development.

The 16-year-old played 13 times last season, but has had to settle for a place on the bench so far this campaign - until now.

He scored two lovely goals at Portman Road to stake his claim for more minutes in the Premier League.

But Arteta warned: "He is 16 years old and we have to be really cautious.

"We don't want to stop him, we don't want to put the brakes on him, we need to develop him and we are fully aware what he needs. He will have opportunities."

His first was a fine solo goal as he ran through, leaving defenders on the floor before slotting in.

"Unbelievable, he's unpredictable, he can go either way, so fluid, so nice to watch," said Arteta.

And for his second goal, Dowman showed good composure to place the ball in the bottom corner.

He is just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side in any competition, after Wayne Rooney for Everton against Wrexham in 2002 - which was also in the League Cup.

"With the demands that we put in them, to be able to do that is extremely difficult and he's coping better and better and better," Arteta added.

"He's an unbelievable player because of the character that he has and how much he loves to play at the biggest stage.

"It's not easy [to contain the hype], I understand, but what we have to do is look after him. He's 16 years old. You don't see that in this league.

"In other leagues in Europe, that's a totally different context, but in this league, with the demands that the league has, the players and everything put on you, we really need to make sure every time we throw him in, he's in the right context with the right preparation."

Wonderkid had to wait

Perhaps Dowman might have expected to have more minutes this season.

His breakthrough came last season as he broke several records.

He became the youngest Champions League player ever, aged 15, Arsenal's youngest ever starter as well as the Premier League's youngest starter, goalscorer and title winner.

In 13 appearances in all competitions, he scored once - against Everton to make a win safe during the title run-in.

In fact his strike, where he ran the ball halfway down the pitch before scoring into an empty net - with Jordan Pickford upfield - was voted Arsenal's goal of the season.

And all of this while he was studying for school exams.

He received his GCSEs from Brentwood School in the summer and left school to focus on his football career.

Sky Sports pundit Jamie Redknapp said: "He is a wonderful player who will be able to do everything in the game.

"But just give him time and how they are handling him is perfect. What you don't want to do is not give him the amount of game time he needs. He is an elite player."

Will Dowman get his chance now?

Breaking into the Arsenal first team will be a tough task for Dowman especially when the Premier League champions are in such fine form.

Arsenal have won all seven games this season, across four competitions.

Dowman was an unused substitute in four of those games, and not involved for the other two, before playing all 90 minutes against Ipswich Town.

The Gunners have played the same attackers in each league game so far - Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz.

But Dowman, especially considering Arteta turned to him in key moments in last season's title race, will hope to gain more of a supporting role.

"He's an unbelievable talent," team-mate Mikel Merino told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He will be a star in the future if he keeps his eyes and ears open and keeps learning.

"He's just 16 so he needs a lot of coaching, especially tactically. But I can't take anything away from him. He's always keen to learn. We'll keep helping him."

Quite possibly the best 16-year-old in the world, it is not unthinkable that he could earn his way into England's Euro 2028 thinking.

In fact there was even a debate about whether he should be going to the World Cup earlier this year.

"He is a real superstar," said former England defender Conor Coady on Sky Sports.

"A 16-year-old boy should not be doing this. He has got no better manager than Arteta to look after him. You want him to be looked after properly. If he plays every game at this age, he won't be scoring goals like this."

And it comes on the day it emerged highly rated 15-year-old striker JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United.

Gabriel had been expected to make his debut in Wednesday's Carabao Cup tie with Brighton.

That will probably deny him the opportunity to break up the stat that the three youngest players to score in the League Cup for a Premier League side all did so for Arsenal.

They are Cesc Fabregas (16y 212d v Wolves, 2003), Dowman (16y 258d v Ipswich) and Jack Wilshere (16y 266d v Sheffield United, 2008).

item.title: Brook likened to Pietersen in SL win - how do they compare?
item.description: Harry Brook hits a brutal century and draws comparisons with Kevin Pietersen as England thrash Sri Lanka by 119 runs in the first T20 in Southampton.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

First Vitality T20, Southampton

England 254-4 (20 overs): Brook 114* (49), Buttler 80 (44)

Sri Lanka 135 (19 overs): Wellalage 33 (21); Baker 3-12

England won by 119 runs

Harry Brook hit a brutal century and drew comparisons with Kevin Pietersen as England thrashed Sri Lanka by 119 runs in the first T20 in Southampton.

The sensational Brook, after a summer without a Test hundred, crashed the ball to all parts in hitting 114 not out from 49 balls to power his side to 254-4.

His 10 fours and six sixes were ferocious - reminiscent of former England batter Pietersen, the newest addition to this side's backroom staff.

His intensity and running between the wickets was equally impressive.

"I don't even think the genius of KP could come close to what Harry Brook has talent-wise," said Brook's former captain and team-mate Ben Stokes, who was watching on TV.

"You are an absolute freak, Harry."

Brook was six years old when Pietersen - a shock appointment as a mentor through to next year's World Cup - secured England the Ashes on the final day at The Oval in 2005.

He was 14, now old enough to understand, when Pietersen was controversially dumped by England after the 2013-14 Ashes defeat.

"I used to love watching him bat when I was younger," said Brook, external - then little more than a year into his international career.

"He always looked to take the attack to bowlers and put them under pressure. In that aspect, I'm quite similar."

How do Brook and Pietersen compare?

Brook is, in many ways, the TikTok generation's Pietersen.

Pietersen invented the switch hit - a shot Brook rarely plays. Brook's version is that tumbling scoop over his and the wicketkeeper's head, which was absent here.

They are most similar in the way they pick length, allowing them to pull, flat-bat or cut balls from spinners even in good areas.

Brook did so throughout his partnership of 128 with Jos Buttler, who also played superbly for his 80 from 44 balls.

And while Pietersen was educated in Pietermaritzburg, South Africa and Brook under the Cumbrian hills, they come from the same cricketing school.

"That's the way I play," Pietersen said after one aggressive shot too many during a Test in 2009.

"I got to 97 playing that way so it obviously wasn't meant to be."

Those words could easily have come from the mouth of Brook.

Such words are why Pietersen and Brook have stirred opinion among England fans more than any other batters in the modern era.

"Is it really that hard to just sit back and admire these players for what they are, on the good days and the bad days, and stop berating them for doing things that we would never, ever, ever even think of doing because we simply aren't on their level to think that way?" Stokes added on social media.

Stokes, who backed Brook to succeed him as Test skipper, has always been a Brook fan.

Picking between Brook and Pietersen may well be pub chat one day, should Brook's career turn out as many hope.

For what it is worth, there is little to choose between their records at Brook's age of 27.

Pietersen's Test average, which ended at 47.28 after his 104 Tests, stood at 49.55 at this stage. Brook's is 53.08, though Pietersen had two more centuries.

Pietersen has the edge in one-day international cricket - an average of 47.87 and six centuries to Brook's 37.43 and three - but the Yorkshireman's second T20 century, hit on the south coast, is two more than Pietersen ever managed.

Perhaps where Brook lags behind is those iconic moments.

While Brook's Test best 317 on a road in Pakistan is a mark few can match, Pietersen's 158 at The Oval won England the 2005 Ashes in his fifth Test.

Eighteen months later he made the same score against Australia in Adelaide against Shane Warne and Glenn McGrath.

Brook's best Ashes score remains 85.

The world's most complete batter?

Still, Brook's latest T20 display showed the company he could one day keep. A more mature batting style in whites this summer has also been noted.

Since being promoted to number three in England's T20 side at the World Cup earlier this year, Brook averages 95.20 at a strike-rate of 200.84.

He has scored 288 runs in the format since he was last dismissed.

"Harry Brook has today cemented himself as maybe the best all-format batter in the world," said former England bowler Steven Finn.

"[Australia's] Travis Head would be up there and so would [India's] Shubman Gill.

"Brook is lacking a Test century in the last year or so but he still averages 42 in that time.

"When you see the versatility of what he did today and the tempo he has played, he's a mighty special player."

Brook also has one clear advantage in any debate for the maverick position in a fantasy England XI.

Overlooked for the Test captaincy, Brook has won 18 of his past 20 T20s as England captain. Pietersen's stint as England skipper lasted only five months.

Sri Lanka's target was always likely to be beyond them but, even without Jofra Archer or Sam Curran, England ruthlessly dismissed their opponents for 135 in Southampton.

Brook oversaw young seamer Sonny Baker's best performance in an England shirt. He took 3-12 in four overs.

"I thought the performance tonight was near perfect," he said afterwards.

England want Pietersen to help them win the 50-over World Cup next year. He will do well to improve on this.

item.title: NI squad only picked on merit - O'Neill
item.description: Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill says he would never take Fifa eligibility rules into consideration when selecting his squad.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill has said he would never take Fifa eligibility rules into consideration when selecting his squad.

Reaching four senior caps for a country rules out a future switch of international allegiance with the regulations again in the spotlight with regards to Arsenal teenager Ceadach O'Neill.

The 18-year-old won his first two Northern Ireland caps in June friendlies against Guinea and France, and is in the squad for an upcoming Nations League quadruple-header, but has also been subject to an approach from the Republic of Ireland.

After stating that he does not feel it is fair to ask teenagers to make "irreversible" decisions on their international future, Michael O'Neill said he would not consider bringing players into the squad with a view to tying them to Northern Ireland before other associations show interest.

"I wouldn't just put a player on the pitch for that because that would be unfair on the player and I've never done that," he said.

"I've never put a player on the pitch from that point of view. I've always tried to be fair across the board if players deserve the opportunity to play, which Ceadach did.

"Because he trained so well, he got the opportunity to play."

Northern Ireland's latest Nations League campaign starts away to Georgia on 25 September and Ceadach O'Neill is one of four teenagers in the squad alongside Blackburn Rovers defender Tom Atcheson, Everton forward Braiden Graham and Kieran Morrison - the Liverpool winger currently on loan at Sheffield Wednesday.

Atcheson and Morrison were both born in England but qualify for Northern Ireland through grandparents and represented the side at underage level before making their senior bows in March and June respectively.

"Kieran deserved the chance to play because he'd been around the Liverpool first team. He'd been showing up well in training as well, both in March and June," said O'Neill after naming a 28-man squad for the four-game window.

"Braiden is the same. They're there because this is the next step for them. I believe being part of the senior international squad will help them, will help their club careers, but they merit a place in a 28-man squad. They merit their place in that squad over some players that aren't in my opinion.

"My job is to protect the national team going forward and to build the squad as strong as possible. To do that you have to look at your young players."

Entrusting young players with key roles, in many cases before they are established at their club sides, has been common practice for Northern Ireland in recent years.

Conor Bradley, Isaac Price and the Charles brothers, Shea and Pierce, all made their international debuts as teenagers, while Sunderland pair Dan Ballard and Trai Hume broke into the side as 20-year-olds.

O'Neill himself won his first cap at 18 in 1988 and cited Norman Whiteside making an international debut as a 17-year-old at the 1982 World Cup as another example of how the side relied on early exposure for young players long before any eligibility issues came to the fore.

"This is not new for Northern Ireland. We've done this in the past," he added.

"I understand how this works. We're doing it based on the level of the player and that's the most important thing."

item.title: Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico
item.description: Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's epic World Cup win against Mexico.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's World Cup win against Mexico.

His Three Lions beat the co-hosts 3-2 in the last-16 tie in July, despite playing much of the second half with 10 men following Jarell Quansah's red card.

England went on to reach the semi-finals, where they lost to Argentina, before beating France in the Bronze medal match for third place.

Tuchel, though, made a bizarre admission during an interview with Daniel Sturridge for the FA's forthcoming feature 'Reflections: England's World Cup Journey'.

He said: "I texted a friend after the match and I just wrote, 'I regret that I didn't eat some grass after the match to keep something from this in my body forever'. That was the feeling. That was the moment.

England's victory was only the third time Mexico had tasted defeat at the stadium in 90 competitive matches.

Tuchel described it as one of the highlights of the campaign and hailed the "huge bond" within the camp, especially the reaction to Jordan Henderson's tournament-ending injury after falling over an advertising hoarding while celebrating the Azteca success.

"This game had so much of what you could wish for," added the German. "If you needed any proof of what it meant to these players and how they were with each other, it was the moment Jordan fell over and broke his arm.

"Within a second, the players were there. Every single player was there stopping the celebrations, building a shield, protecting Jordan, not going anywhere, in full empathy. It was so special."

England are next in action against World Cup winners Spain on 26 September in their 2026-27 Uefa Nations League opener, with the 2028 European Championships also on Tuchel's radar.

Confident of ending England's wait for a first senior men's trophy since 1966, he believed their World Cup run not only cemented his relationship with the squad - "it feels like they are my players now" - but also represented "something to build on".

Tuchel added: "I'm very excited. I think we got another step closer and I think we're there."

item.title: How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
item.description: Kenya's athletics-loving population and improved infrastructure helped Nairobi secure the rights to host the 2029 World Championships, but challenges remain to ensure a successful event.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.

Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.

Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.

After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.

A sport 'woven into the fabric' of the nation

When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".

The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.

The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.

Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.

He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.

A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.

Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.

Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.

Upgraded facilities

Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.

This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.

The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.

"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.

"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.

"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."

Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.

"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.

"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."

President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.

"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.

"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."

Expanding athletics

Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.

During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.

Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.

With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.

"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.

"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.

Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.

London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.

UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.

What is needed next?

Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.

With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.

The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.

There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.

Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.

Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.

"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.

Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.

"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.

Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.

The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.

World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.

In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.

Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.

Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.

The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.

Additional reporting by Ian Williams and Celestine Karoney.

item.title: PGA Tour not planning return program for LIV stars
item.description: PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp says there are no plans to create an instant pathway back for LIV Golf's biggest stars after the breakaway series filed for bankruptcy protection.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

There are no plans to create an instant pathway back to the PGA Tour for LIV Golf's biggest stars.

Major winners Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith are contemplating their futures after LIV filed for bankruptcy protection last week as the breakaway league tries to create a new circuit for next year.

Rahm said he was uncertain about his future plans.

"There's a long legal process they have to go through before a lot of things fall into place," the Spaniard said before playing this week's BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth.

"I really can't give you an answer right now."

The PGA Tour is pressing ahead with its plans for a revamped set-up in 2028 but chief executive Brian Rolapp offered no guarantees that LIV's biggest names will be welcomed back.

"In terms of where we are today, we are not currently contemplating a returning member program like the one you saw in January," Rolapp said.

Brooks Koepka took a deal that brought him back to the US tour at the start of the year but the arrangement was rejected by DeChambeau, Rahm and Smith.

If players abandon LIV, it was thought their most likely route back to the PGA Tour would be through playing the DP World Tour.

Currently, the leading 10 finishers on the Race to Dubai earn cards for the American circuit, but that may change.

Rolapp admitted no deal has been struck over how many DP World Tour players will qualify for his circuit when it splits into a promotion and relegation setup with Championship and Challenger tiers from 2028.

Golfers who defected to LIV were hit with one-year bans that could be served while playing on the DP World Tour. Now it seems there are no guarantees as the revamping of the game's leading circuit continues.

"The PGA Tour is built on meritocracy," Rolapp said. "Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place.

"We are a membership organisation; we have rules, and those rules exist for lots of reasons, including fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter, and they must be enforced."

Rolapp added: "Accountability and discipline, these are essential elements for any sports league and are certainly for the integrity of the PGA Tour and the sport. It's what holds the tour together.

"Those are guiding principles for us."

Negotiations with the DP World Tour over how many players will progress from the European based organisation to the PGA Tour are still to be concluded and the number of cards could be reduced.

"That's very much under discussion both internally and as we continue our discussions with the DP World Tour," Rolapp said.

"The spirit of those conversations are very productive. Both sides are trying to think creatively about how we modify and improve the relationship we have.

"Like any discussions, there's things we agree on, things we don't agree on, things we're trying to work through, and we'll continue to do that."

Rory McIIroy says he is not worried that a deal with the DP World Tour has yet to be concluded, but he warned that cards being made available for the lower Challenger Series would be less attractive.

"I don't see any reason why a DP World Tour player would go to the Challenger Series," said the two-time Masters champion. "I don't see that as an upward move in your career. I see it as a very lateral move."

McIlroy added: "No one's going to argue that the Championship Series is going to be the highest level of tour golf that you can play, and then it's just deciding what an adequate number of cards is to go from here to the Championship Series."

item.title: VAR missed Fernandez offside in Manchester derby - Webb
item.description: Referees' chief Howard Webb admits that the video assistant referee failed to assess the offside offence by Enzo Fernandez for the winning goal in Sunday's Manchester derby.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Referees' chief Howard Webb has admitted that the video assistant referee (VAR) failed to assess the offside offence by Enzo Fernandez for the winning goal in Sunday's Manchester derby.

Speaking on the first edition of 'Match Officials Mic'd Up' of the season, Webb said he was "really disappointed" with the error made by the VAR Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus.

Manchester City striker Erling Haaland thought he had scored the only goal of the game at Old Trafford in the 60th minute, but it was disallowed on the field for offside.

A VAR review found Haaland was just onside, and the goal was awarded.

But it immediately became apparent that the video officials had made an error in failing to identify an offside offence by Fernandez, diving at the ball in a central position and interfering with opponents.

"I was really disappointed with this outcome. We all are," said Webb, Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref's chief refereeing officer.

"None more so than the officials themselves. They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they're obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation.

"They'll not be officiating again until after the international break."

'The VAR gets super-focused on Haaland'

One of the questions which many supporters have asked is how the VAR team could possibly reach the conclusion that Fernandez did not commit an offside offence.

Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez was in close proximity, while goalkeeper Sanne Lammens was positioned for Fernandez to play the ball.

The Mic'd Up audio provided a clear answer. At no stage did Donohue or Antrobus consider it because, as Webb describes, they got "tunnel vision" over Haaland.

The semi-automated offside technology told the VAR that Haaland was three centimetres onside from Josko Gvardiol's cross.

But the video officials then only checked for a touch by Fernandez which would have created a new offside phase against the Norway international.

"The VAR gets super-focused on Haaland," said Webb, who had already been in contact with Manchester United to share the VAR audio and video.

"He establishes he's onside, he thinks that's a good goal.

"He doesn't truly evaluate the full impact of Fernandez's position. He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score.

"In that moment, he gets tunnel vision. It's down to the rest of his team to pull him out of that tunnel, and unfortunately, that didn't happen on this occasion.

"What looks like a really clear subjective offside, because Fernandez doesn't touch the ball but still clearly impacts [the play but] doesn't get identified, and it's really disappointing.

"This goal should've been disallowed. And highly unfortunately, it wasn't, and we'll review it, reflect upon it, and try to take the learning forward to prevent this unusual type of error from happening again."

Fernandes is 'more petulant than violent'

There was also much debate over the red card shown to Phil Foden in the 23th minute for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes, largely because there was no sanction against the Portuguese midfielder for a similar act.

Webb backed the decision to dismiss Foden, but said the action by Fernandes did not meet the threshold for violent conduct.

"I agree with the red card for Phil Foden," said Webb. "He kicks out with force into the upper body of Bruno Fernandes.

"Now, when you look at the footage, there is that petulant kick by Bruno Fernandes into the backside of Foden. It is more petulant than violent.

"To be violent conduct, it has to have excessive force or brutality. When you look at that, particularly in full speed, it doesn't have those elements. So therefore, this would be a yellow card offence."

Webb added that if Foden had not been sent off on the field, but he had been via a VAR review - as Aston Villa's Joao Gomes was at Brighton for a similar offence last month - Fernandes' yellow-card offence would also have been identified at the pitchside monitor.

item.title: The key talking points from Pocognoli's bold Scotland squad
item.description: The Sebastien Pocognoli Scotland era is already creating serious intrigue - and the Belgian's squad are yet to assemble for a training-ground rondo, never mind play a game.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Six new call-ups, seven uncapped players, a refreshed defence, a more-of-the-same midfield and an exciting, new-look attack.

The Sebastien Pocognoli Scotland era is already creating serious intrigue - and the Belgian's squad are yet to assemble for a training-ground rondo, never mind play a game.

The 39-year-old's first taste of competitive action starts with a Nations League opener in Slovenia on 26 September - live on the BBC - beginning an extended four-game international period.

In the meantime, let's dissect the talking points from a bold 28-man selection.

Gunn to continue behind refreshed backline?

There have been no new call-ups in the goalkeeping department. Angus Gunn, now playing with San Jose Earthquakes in the MLS, has 25 caps and will be the favourite to continue between the sticks.

Pocognoli's first selection has shown that a surprise is not beyond him, though. The Belgian stressed the importance of his style in relation to his squad picks, and Falkirk's Scott Bain is a goalkeeper who can deal with the ball at his feet.

Jon McCracken is also playing regularly for Bradford City in England's League One, but Liam Kelly very much remains second choice at Rangers.

As for the backline, the new Scotland boss has predominantly played with a back three throughout his coaching career at both Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco.

He insists on his teams being aggressive in and out of possession, so will want defenders capable of picking brave passes but also with the pace to cover big distances when playing a high line.

Scott McKenna, Jack Hendry and Kieran Tierney all have experience of playing in a back three under Steve Clarke, albeit the approach will differ under Pocognoli. Captain Andy Robertson also clocked up a lot of minutes at left wing-back.

Aaron Hickey, Nathan Patterson and young Colby Donovan, who has impressed Pocognoli "but needs to improve on things like every young lad", are options for the opposite flank.

Uncapped trio Luis Binks, Stephen Welsh and Luke Graham add more depth at centre-back.

Brondby captain Binks, who qualifies for Scotland through a grandparent, has had an interesting career. "The feeling and the timing about him was right," Pocognoli said of the former Bologna and Como man.

At the age of 25, the left-footed centre-back has already played in the MLS, Serie A, English Championship and now Denmark's top tier.

Meanwhile, Stoke's Graham - also left-footed - enjoyed a breakthrough spell at Dundee last season and continues to excel in England's second division, along with Swansea's Welsh, who proved he could thrive in a possession-based Motherwell side last term.

McPake included in familiar midfield

It is much of the same in midfield, although Scott McTominay is absent following a successful heart procedure and Udinese's Lennon Miller is back after being left out of Clarke's World Cup squad.

There is a welcome return for McTominay's Napoli team-mate Billy Gilmour, who suffered a crushing injury just before the start of the finals.

Arguably Scotland's most composed midfielder and best progressive passer, many expect the 25-year-old to thrive in Pocognoli's system. Miller, 20, could also fall into that category.

Experienced campaigners John McGinn, Ryan Christie, Kenny McLean and Lewis Ferguson - the Scots' standout performer earlier this summer - are all included in a seven-man midfield selection, which also features thriving Hearts player Josh McPake.

Signed this summer from St Johnstone, it has been a remarkable rise for the 24-year-old, who has been listed as a midfielder in the squad despite featuring on the left wing for the Tynecastle side. He was a Stirling Albion player just two years ago.

How excited should fans be by new-look attack?

While Ben Gannon-Doak, Findlay Curtis and McPake offer options in attacking wide areas, there is a centre-forward spot up for grabs in the absence of injured pair Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland, plus the omission of Lyndon Dykes.

A free-scoring spell in Sweden earned Robbie Ure the number nine shirt at Sevilla, Oli McBurnie and his Hull team have made an impressive return to the Premier League and Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie scored in a win against Juventus on Sunday.

"Players who are performing well are in the new pathway," Pocognoli said when asked about Rangers academy product Ure, who is yet to score since his switch to La Liga.

"Robbie is adapting well to La Liga. He's put in some good performances, but he maybe needs to adapt to the intensity. Being selected gives him an opportunity."

On the return of McBurnie, who has received his first Scotland call-up in five years, he added: "It's regarding style of play, playing time and performance. I have to start on a new journey, a new book and it's a new opportunity for some players."

The head coach also spoke of his desire to mix youth with the "DNA and heritage" of his squad, evidenced by the inclusion of teenage James Wilson, who is showing signs of fulfilling his serious potential at Hearts.

By the end of the first week in October the Tartan Army, many of whom have been calling for what Pocognoli is preaching to deliver, will have a clearer idea of what that formula is going to look like on the grass, with a fascinating four-match window approaching.

item.title: Draper decides not to play again this season
item.description: Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year.

The 24-year-old has been suffering with bone bruising in his serving arm and has only played nine events since last year's Wimbledon.

Draper missed the US Open, after losing in the first round in Montreal and Cincinnati last month - and was in tears during his defeat to France's Terence Atmane in Canada.

"I am taking this time to reset and heal so when I return I am 100% ready to go," Draper posted on Instagram., external

"Tennis is my purpose and passion and so when I step back on court I want to make sure that there's nothing holding me back from where I want to go."

Draper will not qualify for a protected ranking if he does return in January, as only those who are out for over six months are able to retain the ranking they had when they left the tour.

He is currently ranked 155, which means he would require wildcards or have to come through qualifying to play in Grand Slams and ATP Tour events.

But none of that will worry him if he is able to play freely and without so much pain.

Draper peaked at four in the world last June after winning a first Masters 1000 title in Indian Wells and finishing runner-up at another in Madrid.

"Last summer, all the dedication and work I had put into this sport was coming together," Draper added.

"It was all going my way and the path seemed so clear. However a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging, and since that moment I've been desperately trying to get back and feel as I once did on the court.

"Managing so much change, adversity and pain has helped me to grow massively in many areas of my life but has also made me feel a level of fatigue."

Draper has taken a holiday with friends in recent weeks and has been trying to aid his recovery by taking a mental break from the sport.

He is expected to make a gradual return to training over the next few weeks, as his team try to work out the principal causes of the injury.

Draper making changes as Murray remains part of team - analysis

Draper used to play with polyester strings, but has been experimenting with natural gut - which is against his instincts, but should ease the burden on his arm.

He has also started using a lighter racquet, and is making some changes to his serve. Diet is another area being examined to see if that, too, could be a contributing factor.

Andy Murray remains part of his coaching team but will do a limited number of weeks on the road, and so further assistance will be required.

Over the summer, Draper benefitted from the help of LTA coaches James Trotman (who was with him full-time as he rose into the world's top five) and Alex Lisiecki.

A permanent coach to work alongside Murray will need to be found, however, once Draper returns to the tour.

When he does, much thought will go into his schedule. Not just because the bone bruising is unlikely to have healed entirely by January, but also because of the concerns many top players have about the toll the modern game is putting on their bodies.
